name: pair-fold-right
summary: Folds right over a list's PAIRS rather than its elements, so results come out front-to-back and each step can see everything that follows it.
explanation: pair-fold-right is to fold-right what pair-fold is to fold: the callback receives the pair, not the element, so (car p) is the element and (cdr p) is the whole remaining tail. Because it associates to the right, the accumulator handed to each step is the answer for everything AFTER that position, and the result is built front-to-back with no reverse at the end. That combination makes it the natural verb for anything defined backwards -- distance remaining, tension below, time to finish, run lengths measured forwards -- because each step can either read the tail directly, or read the already-computed answer for the tail and extend it in constant time. Its defining identity is the shortest one in the family: (pair-fold-right cons '() lst) is exactly the list of every suffix of lst, in order, sharing lst's own nodes. If you want the same walk with a left association, or you want to splice while walking, use pair-fold instead.

examples.note: ((1 2 3) (2 3) (3)) -- the one-line definition of "every suffix of a list", in order.
(legs (3 1 4 2) still-to-go (10 7 6 2)) -- how much is left from each point on, and it comes out in travel order.

examples.code:
(define (run-lengths xs)
  (pair-fold-right (lambda (p acc)
                     (cons (if (and (pair? (cdr p)) (< (car p) (cadr p))) (+ 1 (car acc)) 1) acc))
                   '() xs))
(display (run-lengths '(4 7 2 9 9 11 3)))
(newline)
examples.note: (2 1 2 1 2 1 1) -- the rising run starting at each position, in one pass, because each step reads the answer already computed for the tail.

caveats: kons receives a PAIR. Use (car p) for the element and (cdr p) for everything after it.
It associates RIGHT: the accumulator is the answer for the tail, and the result comes out front-to-back with no reverse needed.
The last call is for the final one-element tail, and it receives knil as its accumulator. Test (null? (cdr p)) rather than assuming there is a next element.
Whenever (cdr p) is a pair, acc is non-empty for a cons-building fold. That is what makes the one-pass dynamic-programming shape safe.
(pair-fold-right cons '() lst) is the suffix list of lst, and every suffix in it is lst's own node, not a copy.
It is not the verb for destructive surgery. pair-fold saves each cdr before calling out; reach for that one when the callback will splice.
It is n-ary and stops at the shortest list.
It requires proper lists. A dotted list raises rather than stopping at the improper tail.
usecases: Quantities defined from the end backwards: distance remaining, time to finish, load carried below.
One-pass dynamic programming where each position's answer extends the next position's answer.
Producing the list of all suffixes of a list, which is the verb's defining identity.

learn.concept: Folding right over the pairs gives each step both the tail itself and the answer already computed for that tail, which is exactly the shape of a backwards recurrence.
learn.progression: Write (pair-fold-right cons '() lst) and look at the suffix list it produces. Then compute something over each suffix independently and notice it is quadratic. Then rewrite it so each step extends the accumulator instead of re-reading the tail, and watch the same answer come out in one pass.

provenance: SRFI-1 (fold, unfold and map: pair-fold-right); record authored 2026-08-04

row-2-audit.math-program:
(define (later-max xs)
  (pair-fold-right (lambda (p acc)
                     (cons (if (null? (cdr p)) 'none (apply max (cdr p))) acc))
                   '() xs))
(display (list 'rising (later-max '(1 2 3))
               'falling (later-max '(3 2 1))
               'one (later-max '(5))))
(newline)
row-2-audit.cs-program:
(define (suffix-report xs)
  (let ((ss (pair-fold-right cons '() xs)))
    (list 'count (length ss)
          'lengths (map length ss)
          'shared (map (lambda (s i) (eq? s (list-tail xs i))) ss (iota (length ss))))))
(display (list 'three (suffix-report '(a b c))
               'one (suffix-report '(z))
               'none (suffix-report '())))
(newline)
row-2-audit.problem: A route planner has a list of leg distances and must report, at every waypoint, how far there still is to go. Candidates: pair-fold-right (one traversal, the tail is right there, and the answers come out in travel order with no reverse), pair-fold plus a reverse (the same walk with an extra pass and an easy off-by-one when the reverse is forgotten), fold-right carrying a running total (correct and linear, and the real competitor -- it needs the accumulator to hold both the total and the list being built, which is two jobs in one slot), map over (list-tail legs i) for each i (quadratic and it recomputes the tails the list already contains), a reversed running sum with fold (works, and the reader has to hold the list backwards in their head to check it). pair-fold-right is the pick because the quantity is defined from the end backwards and the output is wanted from the front forwards, which is precisely the direction mismatch this verb removes.
row-2-audit.explanation: eng: distance still to go from each leg onward, over four legs, one leg, and none -- the single-leg case answers with that leg's own distance because there is nothing after it, and the empty case answers the empty list rather than zero. math: the largest value strictly after each position, over a rising list, a falling list, and a single element; the last position has nothing after it and says so instead of inventing a number. cs: the suffix list reported as a count, its lengths, and whether each suffix is the input's own node -- which is what distinguishes the real verb from one that rebuilds the tails.
row-2-audit.meta: The shared field in the cs program is the load-bearing check. A version that consed fresh tails would produce identical counts and identical lengths, and every test that only reads values would pass. Only eq? against the list's own tails tells them apart.
row-2-audit.eng: Distance-remaining is defined from the destination backwards but consumed from the start forwards. Any implementation has to reconcile those two directions, and the only question is whether it costs a reverse.
row-2-audit.math: The maximum over the strict suffix is the running maximum from the right. Reporting a symbol rather than a number at the last position keeps the function total instead of raising on an empty max.
row-2-audit.cs: A suffix list that shares structure costs no allocation at all -- it is n conses for the spine and nothing else. A copying version costs quadratic space and nobody notices until the list is long.

row-3-dimension.setup: Folding right over a list's tails instead of its elements.

rungs.domain: a hanging chain where each link carries the weight of everything below it
rungs.code:
(define chain '((hook 0) (a 4) (b 3) (c 7) (d 2)))
(define (tensions links)
  (pair-fold-right (lambda (p acc)
                     (cons (list (car (car p)) (apply + (map cadr p))) acc))
                   '() links))
(display (list 'tensions (tensions chain)
               'worst (apply max (map cadr (tensions chain)))))
(newline)

rungs.domain: a build pipeline where each stage's time to finish extends the next stage's, computed in a single pass
rungs.code:
(define stages '((fetch 2) (compile 9) (link 3) (test 5) (package 1)))
(define (time-to-finish ss)
  (pair-fold-right (lambda (p acc)
                     (cons (list (car (car p))
                                 (+ (cadr (car p)) (if (null? acc) 0 (cadr (car acc)))))
                           acc))
                   '() ss))
(display (list 'schedule (time-to-finish stages)
               'total (cadr (car (time-to-finish stages)))))
(newline)

row-3-dimension.explanation: On bare numbers the fold reads the tail and reduces it, and the accumulator is only a place to put the answer. On the hanging chain it does the same thing with meaning attached -- each link sums the weights below it -- and because every step re-reads its whole tail the walk is quadratic in the number of links. In the build pipeline the step stops reading the tail at all: it reads the ACCUMULATOR, which already holds the answer for the next stage, and adds its own cost. Same fold, same output shape, and the work per step drops from the length of the tail to a constant. That is the whole reason the right-associating version exists.
row-3-dimension.meta: Rungs two and three compute the same kind of quantity and differ only in what each step looks at. Rung two would still be correct if the accumulator were discarded; rung three would still be correct if the tail were discarded. Reaching for the accumulator is what turns a quadratic definition into a linear program, and it is available only because this fold associates to the right.
row-3-dimension.eng: Tension at a link is the load below it, which is why chains fail at the top. Computing it from the bottom up is the definition; computing it in one pass is the implementation.
row-3-dimension.math: Both rungs are the same backwards recurrence, T(i) = w(i) + T(i+1), written two ways. Expanding the recurrence at every position is the quadratic form; carrying it is the linear form.
row-3-dimension.cs: A right fold's accumulator is the answer for the rest of the input. Recognising that turns a large family of 'for each suffix' definitions into single-pass programs without any memo table.

row-4-proof.eng-program:
(define (suffix-list-is-tails? xs)
  (let ((ss (pair-fold-right cons '() xs)))
    (and (= (length ss) (length xs))
         (let loop ((s ss) (i 0))
           (cond ((null? s) #t)
                 ((eq? (car s) (list-tail xs i)) (loop (cdr s) (+ i 1)))
                 (else #f))))))
(display (map suffix-list-is-tails? '(() (a) (a b) (1 2 3 4 5) ((x) (y)))))
(newline)
row-4-proof.math-program:
(define (agrees-with-fold-right? xs)
  (and (equal? (pair-fold-right (lambda (p acc) (cons (car p) acc)) '() xs)
               (fold-right cons '() xs))
       (equal? (pair-fold-right (lambda (p acc) (cons (car p) acc)) '() xs) xs)
       (equal? (pair-fold-right cons '() xs)
               (reverse (pair-fold cons '() xs)))))
(display (map agrees-with-fold-right? '(() (1) (1 2 3) (a b) ((1 2) (3)))))
(newline)
row-4-proof.cs-program:
(define (suffix-chain-ok? xs)
  (let ((ss (pair-fold-right cons '() xs)))
    (and (equal? (map length ss) (reverse (iota (length xs) 1)))
         (let loop ((s ss))
           (cond ((null? s) #t)
                 ((null? (cdr s)) (null? (cdr (car s))))
                 ((eq? (cdr (car s)) (cadr s)) (loop (cdr s)))
                 (else #f))))))
(display (map suffix-chain-ok? '(() (a) (a b c) (1 2 3 4 5 6) ((p) (q) (r)))))
(newline)
row-4-proof.claim: (pair-fold-right cons '() x) is the list of x's suffixes: it has one entry per element, the i-th entry is x's own i-th tail, the entries' lengths run n down to 1, and each entry's cdr is the next entry with the last entry's cdr empty. Using only (car p) it computes exactly what fold-right computes, and it is the reverse of what pair-fold sees.
row-4-proof.invariant: For all proper lists x of length n: pair-fold-right(cons, (), x) = (t_0 ... t_{n-1}) where t_i eq? list-tail(x, i); length(t_i) = n - i; cdr(t_i) eq? t_{i+1} for i < n-1 and cdr(t_{n-1}) = (); pair-fold-right(lambda (p a) (kons (car p) a), z, x) = fold-right(kons, z, x); and pair-fold-right(cons, (), x) = reverse(pair-fold(cons, (), x))
row-4-proof.meta: Three claims: the suffixes are the list's own nodes, the walk agrees with fold-right on (car p), and the two pair folds see the same pairs in opposite order. What would falsify them: a copied tail, an off-by-one that dropped the one-element tail or added an empty one, a left association masquerading as a right one, or the two family members disagreeing about which pairs exist. The empty list appears in all three programs because it is where an off-by-one shows first.
row-4-proof.eng: Structure sharing is the whole economy of the suffix list: n conses, no copying, and every suffix usable as a live handle into the original. Proving eq? against list-tail is what licenses treating it that way.
row-4-proof.math: Restricted to (car p), pair-fold-right IS fold-right, with the same associativity and the same argument order. That containment is why the wider verb needs no separate mental model.
row-4-proof.cs: Checking pair-fold-right against reverse of pair-fold ties the two verbs to one another. Either could be individually plausible and still disagree about the last tail, and nothing that inspects only values would notice.

row-5-emergence.eng-composition:
(define (suffix-totals xs)
  (pair-fold-right (lambda (p acc) (cons (apply + p) acc)) '() xs))
(define (refuel-plan legs range)
  (let loop ((ls legs) (rem (suffix-totals legs)) (tank range) (i 0) (stops '()))
    (cond ((null? ls) (list 'stops (reverse stops) 'left tank))
          ((> (car ls) range) (list 'impossible i))
          ((< tank (car ls))
           (let ((fill (if (<= (car rem) range) (car rem) range)))
             (loop ls rem fill i (cons (list i 'fill fill) stops))))
          (else (loop (cdr ls) (cdr rem) (- tank (car ls)) (+ i 1) stops)))))
(display (list 'tight (refuel-plan '(3 4 2 5 1) 6)
               'roomy (refuel-plan '(3 4 2 5 1) 20)
               'toosmall (refuel-plan '(3 4 2 5 1) 4)))
(newline)
row-5-emergence.math-composition:
(define (tails xs) (pair-fold-right cons '() xs))
(define (suffix-maxima xs) (map (lambda (t) (apply max t)) (tails xs)))
(define (leaders xs)
  (let loop ((ts (tails xs)) (out '()))
    (if (null? ts)
        (reverse out)
        (loop (cdr ts)
              (let ((t (car ts)))
                (if (or (null? (cdr t)) (> (car t) (apply max (cdr t))))
                    (cons (car t) out)
                    out))))))
(display (list 'maxima (map suffix-maxima '((1 3 2) (5 4 3)))
               'leaders (map leaders '((16 17 4 3 5 2) (1 2 3) (7)))))
(newline)
row-5-emergence.cs-composition:
(define (tails xs) (pair-fold-right cons '() xs))
(define (common-suffix a b)
  (let loop ((ta (reverse (tails a))) (tb (reverse (tails b))) (best '()))
    (if (or (null? ta) (null? tb))
        best
        (if (eq? (car ta) (car tb)) (loop (cdr ta) (cdr tb) (car ta)) best))))
(define (sharing-report a b)
  (let ((c (common-suffix a b)))
    (list 'shared c 'depth (length c) 'of-a (if (null? a) 0 (/ (length c) (length a))))))
(define tailseg (list 3 4 5))
(define aa (cons 1 (cons 2 tailseg)))
(define bb (cons 9 tailseg))
(display (list 'overlap (sharing-report aa bb)
               'none (sharing-report '(1 2) '(3 4))
               'identical (sharing-report aa aa)))
(newline)
row-5-emergence.base: pair-fold-right walks a list's tails right to left and emits results left to right, and with cons it emits the tails themselves.
row-5-emergence.emergent: eng: suffix-totals is one pair-fold-right; refuel-plan drives a vehicle along the legs and, whenever the tank runs short, fills only as much as the rest of the trip actually needs -- which requires knowing the remaining distance at every waypoint, and answers three different questions for three tank sizes including an impossible one. math: tails is one pair-fold-right; suffix-maxima reduces each tail and leaders keeps every element bigger than everything after it, which is the classic 'leaders in an array' problem stated exactly as its definition. cs: tails is one pair-fold-right; common-suffix walks two suffix lists from the short end comparing them with eq?, and sharing-report turns that into how much structure two lists physically share.
row-5-emergence.meta: The cs composition is the one that could not be written any other way. equal? would report a common suffix between two lists that merely look alike; eq? on the tails reports the nodes they actually share, which is a fact about memory rather than about values. The 'none' case is two lists with no shared node at all, and the 'identical' case is a list against itself where the shared depth is the whole thing. Every larger function here calls its helper and cannot run without it.
row-5-emergence.eng: Filling only what the rest of the trip needs is a real optimisation and it is impossible without the remaining-distance table. Topping up to full every time is the version that carries dead weight to the destination.
row-5-emergence.math: An element is a leader when it exceeds the maximum of its strict suffix. Written from the suffix list it is the definition; written with a running maximum it is linear, and having the definition on hand is how the linear one gets checked.
row-5-emergence.cs: Shared structure is invisible to equal? and central to how functional data structures stay cheap. Measuring it needs eq? on the actual tails, which is exactly what the suffix list hands over.
